answer:
Your colleague's claim is too broad. Both archetypes start with a quick fix that relieves a symptom. They differ in what the fix damages later.

## The test

Ask what the quick fix does a few rounds from now.

| | **Fixes That Fail** | **Shifting the Burden** |
|---|---|---|
| What the fix damages | The **problem itself**. The side effect makes the underlying problem worse. | The **capability to apply a better fix**. It atrophies from disuse. |
| Is there a competing fundamental fix? | Not required. | Required. A slower fix that could resolve the root cause must exist. |
| Structure | A fast balancing loop (the fix) sits on a slower reinforcing loop that the fix feeds. | Two balancing loops (quick and fundamental) close the same gap, and a reinforcing "capability erosion" loop connects them. |
| Why it recurs | The problem is genuinely larger, so you need more of the same fix. | The fundamental fix keeps looking harder and further off, so the quick fix keeps winning. |
| Diagnostic question | Does the problem come back **worse** after each round, as if the fix were feeding it? | Is the fix **crowding out** a fundamental one while the ability to do that one fades? |
| Intervention | Use the fix as a bridge. Work on why performance slipped, and expose the delayed side effect early. | Rebuild the fundamental capability now. Keep the stopgap, but spend the time it buys exercising the fading skill. |

Each archetype can be used wrongly in a specific way:
- **Fixes That Fail** needs a side effect of the fix itself that feeds the problem. A fix that simply didn't work doesn't count.
- **Shifting the Burden** needs both a real fundamental alternative and an erosion of the ability to apply it. A quick fix alone doesn't count.

Before naming either, trace the links. Check that the loop polarities match the archetype's. Don't diagnose from how familiar the story sounds.

## Example: Fixes That Fail

A support team is behind on tickets, so everyone works overtime.

- Backlog drops right away. That is the fast balancing loop.
- Fatigue builds over weeks. People make more mistakes and quit.
- Errors create reopened tickets and rework, and attrition shrinks the team.
- The backlog grows, so management asks for more overtime.

The fix directly worsens the problem it was meant to solve. There is no better skill that overtime displaced. The overtime itself produces the extra work. The leverage point is to measure burnout and rework directly so the delay disappears. Overtime can serve as a short bridge while you address why the backlog grew.

## Example: Shifting the Burden

Every time a service gets slow, the team calls the one engineer who knows the system and they restart it or tune it by hand.

- The slowness goes away within minutes. That is the quick fix.
- The fundamental fix is to fix the architecture and write runbooks so anyone can diagnose the cause.
- Because the hero always solves it, nobody else learns the system and the root-cause work never gets scheduled.
- Each incident makes the proper fix look harder, because fewer people can do it. The next incident leads to another call to the hero.

The workaround doesn't make the slowness worse. It starves the capability that could cure the slowness. This is the intervenor variant of the archetype, because the quick fix is a specific person. The leverage point is to rebuild the fading capability now. Pair others with the hero, write the runbooks, and keep the manual restart only as a stopgap. Don't ban it, because the symptom is real.

## Reply to your colleague

Both involve quick fixes, but they fail in different ways:
- If the quick fix **makes the problem worse**, it's Fixes That Fail.
- If it **makes the better fix harder to reach**, it's Shifting the Burden.
- If it does neither, it may be a perfectly good quick fix. With a short delay or a weak side effect, the fix just works.
